---
title: "Uncertainty Is Probability"
---



A forecast is not a number — it is a **distribution**.  A point estimate throws
away exactly the thing risk cares about: how wrong you might be, and in which
direction.

## A Point Estimate Hides the Tail

A model that reports "expected return = $\mu$" — or even a tidy 95% band that
assumes thin Gaussian tails — can look fine right up until the loss that lands far
out in a tail it never represented.

::: {#cell-fig-honest-forecast .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
grid = np.linspace(-8, 8, 600)
confident = norm.pdf(grid, 0, 1.0)
honest = student_t.pdf(grid, df=2.5)
realized = -4.6

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
ax.fill_between(grid, confident, color=WARM, alpha=0.35, label="confident (Gaussian)")
ax.plot(grid, honest, c=INK, lw=2.2, label="honest (fat-tailed)")
ax.axvline(0, color=WARM, lw=1.4, ls="--", label="point forecast")
ax.axvline(realized, color=CRASH, lw=2.0, label="realized loss")
ax.set_xlabel("return"); ax.set_ylabel("probability density")
ax.set_title("The point forecast is the least useful summary", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False)
despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![A confident point forecast (and a thin Gaussian band) versus the honest, fat-tailed predictive distribution. The realized loss lands where the confident view assigned almost no probability.](01-uncertainty-is-probability_files/figure-html/fig-honest-forecast-output-1.png){#fig-honest-forecast width=945 height=489}
:::
:::


## Uncertainty Has a Number: Entropy

Surprise is $\log\frac{1}{p(x)}$; **entropy** is its average,
$H(X) = \mathbb E[\log\frac{1}{p(X)}]$ — the [same quantity](../dependence/02-mutual-information.qmd)
from the dependence chapter, here measuring *how unsure* a forecast is.

::: {#cell-fig-entropy-ladder .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def entropy_bits(p):
    p = np.asarray(p, float)
    return float(-(p[p > 0] * np.log2(p[p > 0])).sum())

dists = {
    "near-certain": np.array([0.85, 0.08, 0.05, 0.02]),
    "moderate": np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05]),
    "max uncertainty": np.array([0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25]),
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.6))
for ax, (name, p) in zip(axes, dists.items()):
    ax.bar(range(4), p, color=COOL, alpha=0.85)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nH = {entropy_bits(p):.2f} bits", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_xticks(range(4))
    ax.set_xticklabels(["A", "B", "C", "D"]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Three forecasts over the same outcomes, from near-certain to maximally uncertain. Entropy puts a number on it.](01-uncertainty-is-probability_files/figure-html/fig-entropy-ladder-output-1.png){#fig-entropy-ladder width=1424 height=418}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The Axiom — Claim Only What Your Evidence Justifies

The honest forecast is the **most uncertain** (maximum-entropy) distribution
consistent with what you actually know.  A corollary that surprises people:
**learning does not only shrink uncertainty.**  Evidence that conflicts with your
model can *widen* the predictive distribution (and shift it) — being well
calibrated sometimes means becoming *less* sure.  The Gaussian is the
least-committal joint for a given mean and covariance, which is exactly why
[Gaussianization](../gaussianization/index.qmd) is the natural reference.
:::

## Discrete and Continuous, One Idea

For discrete outcomes, probability is a table that sums to one; for continuous
ones, a density that integrates to one.  Both carry the same uncertainty content,
and both transform by the **same rule** when pushed through a model — the subject
of the [next page](02-probability-under-transformation.qmd).
